levels.name: Beginner
levels.body: Major in C, F and G (written), A minor toward the end. One octave, calm and even (♩ ≈ 60–72). Tone before technique.
tips: Long tones first: 8+ beats per note with a calm, steady airstream or bow.
Sing the scale before you play it — hear the note before you make it.
Use a mirror and listen: an even tone on every note matters more than tempo.
brassTips: Long tones first: 8+ beats on G4 and C4 (low C) with a calm, open airstream.
Lip slurs on the open partials (C4–G4–C5) without valves before the scale.
Sing or “buzz” the scale on the mouthpiece before you play it.

levels.name: Intermediate
levels.body: Major up to 3–4 sharps or flats (the band keys), minor in harmonic and melodic form, the chromatic scale, the dominant seventh. Eighth notes ♩ ≈ 80–100, both slurred and articulated.
tips: Practice the scale slurred first, then articulated at the same tempo — always with a metronome.
Practice from the top down as well — the descent reveals unevenness.
Plan your breathing/bowing: the last note as full as the first.
brassTips: Daily lip slurs (Arban/Schlossberg) on all valve combinations.
Practice the scale slurred first, then tongued at the same tempo — always with a metronome.
Plan your breathing: at most one breath per octave run, and the last note as full as the first.

levels.name: Advanced
levels.body: All 12 major and minor keys from memory, arpeggios (major, minor, dom7, dim7). Two octaves where the range allows. Sixteenth notes ♩ ≈ 80–112, mixed articulations.
tips: Practice the scales in patterns of thirds and with rhythmic variations as well.
Two octaves come from control and relaxation — not force.
The modes: same key signature, new starting point — hear the difference.
brassTips: Practice the scales from the top down too, and in patterns of thirds.
Two octaves come from air support and flexibility — not mouthpiece pressure.
The modes: same key signature, new starting point — hear the difference.

levels.name: Professional
levels.body: All keys in all modes, jazz and symmetric scales, pattern studies through the entire range — in all articulations and dynamics.
tips: Rotate: one key per day, through all modes and arpeggios.
Practice in all dynamics — pianissimo reveals the most.
Transpose etudes: think concert and written pitch at the same time.
brassTips: Clarke study no. 2 through all keys — pianissimo and effortless.
Rotate: one key per day, through all modes and arpeggios.
Transpose etudes: think concert and written pitch at the same time.

theory.tKvintTitle: How to read the circle of fifths
theory.tKvint:
The circle of fifths arranges all keys by how many sharps or flats are in their key signature. One step clockwise is a perfect fifth up — and one more sharp (or one flat fewer). One step counterclockwise is a fifth down — one more flat.

Neighboring keys share six of their seven notes and therefore sound closely related. That is why the dominant (D) — the fifth above — and the subdominant (S) — the fifth below — are the most important chord functions next to the tonic.

The outer and inner ring at the same position share a key signature: these are relative keys (e.g. {exMajor} and {exMinor}). At the bottom of the circle the sharp and flat sides meet in the enharmonic keys: the same sounding pitches, two ways of writing them.
theory.tFortegnTitle: Key signatures: order and all keys
theory.tFortegn:
The sharps always appear in the order {sharpOrder} (rising in fifths). The flats appear in the opposite order: {flatOrder} (falling in fifths).

Two useful rules of thumb: the last sharp is a half step below the tonic of the major key (the leading tone). The second-to-last flat is the major key.
theory.tParallell:
In English theory, the relative key is the major or minor key that shares the same key signature, with tonics a minor third apart: {exKey} ↔ {exRel}. (Beware in translation: German and Scandinavian theory calls this the “parallel key” — a false friend!)

The parallel key is major and minor on the same tonic, e.g. {exVar1} and {exVar2} — same tonic, but three accidentals apart. (In Germanic terminology this is the “variant key.”)

Minor comes in three forms: natural (as its relative major), harmonic (raised 7th degree — providing a leading tone and a characteristic augmented second) and melodic (raised 6th and 7th degrees ascending; the natural form descending in the classical tradition).
theory.tTranspTransposing: {instr} is a transposing instrument: a written C sounds as {soundsNote} — {interval} {direction}. To obtain a desired sounding pitch, you therefore write {interval} {oppositeDirection}.
theory.tTranspNon: {instr} is non-transposing: the written note and the sounding pitch are the same. The table below still shows how transposing instruments relate to concert pitch.
theory.tTranspTable: The same principle applies to the rest of the orchestra: clarinet in B♭ (a major second up), French horn in F (a perfect fifth up), alto saxophone in E♭ (a major sixth up), double bass (an octave up). Rule of thumb: the instrument's name is the pitch that sounds when it plays a written C.
theory.tIntonasjon:
The valves lower the pitch by fixed lengths of tubing, but combinations come out too short — so some fingerings are systematically out of tune:

1·3 and 1·2·3 are sharp. Written {noteD4} (1·3) and {noteCiss4} (1·2·3) are the notorious ones: extend the 3rd-valve slide (about 1–1.5 cm for 1·3, 2–2.5 cm for 1·2·3).

The 5th partial is flat. Written {noteE5} with the open fingering sits ~14 cents flat — adjust with the lips, or use 1·2 (6th partial) as an alternate fingering.

The 7th partial is avoided. Open {noteB5} sits ~31 cents flat and is used only for jazz effects (the “shake”) — play it with the 1st valve.

The 3rd valve alone ≈ 1·2 and serves as an alternate fingering for trills and intonation ({alt3list}).
